# Preface {#sec-about .unnumbered}

## Who This Book Is For {#sec-about-audience}

This book is for senior undergraduates and beginning graduate students in computer science, robotics, electrical engineering, and machine learning, and for practicing engineers who build, deploy, or certify physical AI systems. It is written for the engineer who has watched an embodied policy succeed in simulation or a scripted demonstration and now has to ship a machine that moves mass among people, day after day. That machine must not collide with a coworker, damage a payload, burn out a motor winding, or run away on a network timeout.

The reader should understand basic programming in Python and machine learning intuition, and be comfortable with introductory Newtonian physics, linear algebra, and basic probability. The book assumes no prior book in this series. It develops physical AI concepts where they are first used and derives the timing, control, and hardware-placement relationships needed to reason about embodied workloads without requiring specialist background in nonlinear control theory or application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) microarchitecture.

## Why a Physical AI Systems Textbook {#sec-about-why}

A reasonable engineer might look at the current wave of robot foundation models and ask a skeptical question. *Is physical artificial intelligence a genuine systems discipline with durable principles, or is it simply classical robotics with a transformer bolted on, or an end-to-end neural network running on an onboard computer?*

The skepticism is fair. Much of what is written about embodied AI highlights impressive single-task demonstrations, such as a dexterous hand folding laundry or a humanoid walking through a lab. Demonstration, however, is not deployment. In the field, failure rarely comes from the raw expressiveness of the model. What fails is the system around it, as when an observation arrives 50 milliseconds too late, an action proposal demands more torque than the joint drives can deliver, or an unmodeled delay turns a braking command into an impact.

Traditional machine learning systems center on disembodied prediction. A model evaluates static inputs in an open loop and returns advisory labels, rankings, or tokens without acting directly on the world. Because a person or downstream service must still decide what to do with that output, an erroneous prediction can be discarded or recalculated before it causes harm, and systems engineering centers on balancing training cost against serving latency, memory, and throughput. Agentic machine learning systems move from single predictions to sequential action: a model formulates multi-step plans, inspects feedback, and invokes software tools in a closed loop. As long as that loop stays inside a digital environment, however, virtual time can be paused, execution can be sandboxed, and failed transactions can be rolled back.

Physical AI systems bring agency into continuous physics. When an autonomous model commands actuators, computation crosses the causal boundary into mass, momentum, friction, and heat. In continuous physics, virtual sandboxes do not exist: time cannot pause while a foundation model deliberates, and Newtonian work cannot be rolled back after an impact. A larger model cannot shorten a stopping distance, cool an electric winding, or recover clearance spent while it computed. Physical AI therefore requires an architectural discipline. Learned models propose, while an independent permission path, with its own timing and its own fallback, decides what may cross into the physical world.

This book teaches how to design, measure, and govern that machine. Its central question is what an embodied task needs around a learned model to produce useful physical service supported by the required evidence. Readers should leave able to translate physical limits into computational budgets, design sensorimotor policies that close the loop under real-time deadlines, enforce runtime assurance independently of the learned proposer, and justify release through an assurance case that links claims to empirical evidence.

## The Causal Boundary and the Four Laws {#sec-about-mental-model}

The unit of engineering in this book is the **causal boundary**, the interface where an admitted digital command becomes current in a motor winding, torque on a shaft, and physical force delivered to the world. Accuracy on a held-out dataset is not the measure of a physical AI system. The measure is whether closed-loop actions achieve task goals within verified physical limits, supported by evidence independent of the learned model's self-report, and at what cost in latency, energy, thermal margin, and compute.

Four governing laws anchor the book's architecture. Each law pairs a physical or statistical constraint with the systems mechanism required to bound it:

- **The First Law: Irreversibility.** Software cannot roll back physical consequences. Every check that admits a command must finish before the machine spends its remaining clearance, so physical limits become strict budgets in time, distance, torque, heat, and voltage.
- **The Second Law: Endogenous Data.** A physical machine's actions choose its next observations. The states a deployed policy visits are conditioned on its own previous actions, so competence is a claim bounded by the operating envelope that closed-loop evaluation actually verified.
- **The Third Law: Proposal Is Not Permission.** A learned model may propose motion; only an independent permission path may admit it. The permission path evaluates state whose age is bounded, executes within a deterministic deadline set by the plant physics, and maintains a feasible fallback that does not depend on the learned proposer.
- **The Fourth Law: Permission Must Be Earned.** Permission to operate is granted per operating condition on recorded evidence, and it expires when that evidence does.

The first of these is a physical law. The other three are design principles, the embodied counterparts to covariate shift, runtime assurance, and the assurance case. This book elevates them to bedrock laws because a production machine that violates them incurs predictable physical risks.

Two relations quantify these obligations throughout the book. **Delay is distance** governs the stopping budget: if a machine moving at velocity $\SpeedAtDetection$ takes reaction time $\PrebrakeDelay$ to sense, compute, and actuate before decelerating at rate $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration$, the total stopping distance is $\StoppingDistance = \SpeedAtDetection \cdot \PrebrakeDelay + \frac{\SpeedAtDetection^2}{2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration}$. Every millisecond of latency is distance spent before braking can begin. **Evidence expiration** governs the validity of state: an observation or state estimate carries an expiration timestamp derived from the plant's maximum rate of change, after which it cannot justify a safety assertion.

The machine's architecture separates five roles: the **Brain** (learned models that propose goals and motion), the **Nervous System** (deterministic communication and the independent permission path), the **Body** (drives, transmissions, windings, and power systems), the **Boundary** (register writes and sensor captures), and the **World** (continuous physical dynamics, obstacles, and people). A warehouse mobile manipulator that navigates an aisle shared with workers, opens a spring-latched door, and handles a fragile payload serves as the running reference machine in every chapter. A humanoid example at the end of each part tests whether the reasoning survives a body that couples balance, joint torque, and thermal dissipation.

## What This Book Covers {#sec-about-covers}

The book builds understanding in physical dependency order: **anatomy, teaching, running, governing**. Each part adds responsibilities that the preceding material prepares the reader to evaluate, and reference appendices supply the supporting mathematical, control, and hardware derivations:

- **Introduction: The Causal Boundary** (@sec-boundary) prices delay at the causal boundary, defines the five-level machine architecture, and establishes the four governing laws.
- **Part I: The Machine Anatomy** turns the first law into physical budgets. @Sec-body measures what the body can do before damage, @sec-brain characterizes the learned proposer and how quickly its evidence ages, and @sec-nervous derives how frequently the permission path must tick and how long a proposal may drive the actuators.
- **Part II: Teaching the Machine** applies the second law to sensorimotor learning. @Sec-data records demonstrations with their operating conditions, @sec-training analyzes training regimes and the dependencies they hide, and @sec-evaluation bounds the policy's competence through finite-trial closed-loop evaluation.
- **Part III: Running the Machine** applies the third law at runtime. It follows dated sensor measurements through perception (@sec-perception), spatial memory and state estimation (@sec-memory), intent grounding (@sec-intent), and trajectory planning (@sec-planning) to runtime enforcement (@sec-enforcement), and tests whether real-time hardware keeps that path on time (@sec-placement).
- **Part IV: Governing the Machine** applies the fourth law to operational authority. @Sec-intervention governs how authority passes between the machine and an operator. @Sec-verification injects physical and computational faults to prove containment. @Sec-release constructs the assurance case that justifies release under named conditions. @Sec-responsibility names who answers for each decision behind an admitted action, which human roles a person can actually perform, and which people bear the machine's risk and appear in its records.
- **Conclusion: Engineering Physical AI** (@sec-frontier) synthesizes the complete methodology, transfers the reasoning to an unfamiliar machine, and establishes the open research frontier.

Reference appendices provide background on machine learning foundations (@sec-appendix-ml), control and dynamics (@sec-appendix-control), systems and hardware (@sec-appendix-systems), sensorimotor troubleshooting (@sec-appendix-spa-troubleshooting), and a unified glossary. Each appendix is organized as a lookup reference so that readers can consult a specific derivation without losing the thread of the main text.

## How to Read This Book {#sec-about-reading}

The book is written to be read in order. Each chapter uses only ideas introduced earlier or defined where they appear, and each owns its concepts. Every chapter opens with the physical problem it solves, develops the mechanism as the answer, and closes with a summary and a handoff to the next chapter. Classical systems mechanisms (watchdog leases, safety filters, interlocks, fail-safe fallbacks, and real-time scheduling) appear as concrete solutions to physical hazards rather than as abstract theory.

Readers with a particular focus can tailor their depth after the introduction. Four tracks correspond to the primary engineering roles that collaborate on a physical AI deployment:

- **Core systems curriculum**: Follow the complete sequence from @sec-boundary through @sec-frontier to integrate physical limits, learning, runtime design, and operational evidence.
- **ML systems and learned runtimes**: Focus on the common foundation, sensorimotor training and evaluation (@sec-data through @sec-evaluation), perception and planning (@sec-perception through @sec-placement), and release (@sec-release).
- **Embedded systems and silicon**: Focus on the common foundation, runtime placement (@sec-placement), communication timing (@sec-nervous), and fault verification (@sec-verification).
- **Robotics, control, and assurance**: Focus on the common foundation, state estimation and planning (@sec-memory through @sec-planning), runtime enforcement (@sec-enforcement), human intervention (@sec-intervention), and responsibility for the people around the machine (@sec-responsibility).

Evidence flows from physical anatomy through training and runtime execution to operational release, and the chapter dependencies across the six divisions of the book follow that progression (@fig-vol4-chapter-dependencies). Every arrow in the map represents a concrete record or physical bound handed forward from one engineering stage to the next.

### Marginal reading aids and navigation pointers {#sec-about-margin-pointers}

The margins carry small visual aids beside the prose where a quantitative relationship, scale gap, or threshold is easiest to see. Each visual follows one of five recurring forms:

- **Ladders** span orders of magnitude (such as sensor ingestion bandwidths or execution loop rates).
- **Threshold knees** mark the point where a physical relationship changes regime (such as reflected rotor inertia dominating gear trains or contact stiffness spiking forces).
- **Budget envelopes** set competing demands against a deadline (such as diffusion denoising steps against control periods, or operator takeover latencies).
- **Sequence strips** illustrate multi-phase timing (such as receding-horizon chunk execution or fault handshakes).
- **Causal chains** trace fault propagation from sensor error to physical consequence.

![](/vol4/06_training/images/svg/margin_generative_inference_deadlines_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Margin visual example: budget envelope contrasting denoising times against control deadlines."}

![](/vol4/14_intervention/images/svg/margin_takeover_allowance_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Margin visual example: budget envelope setting takeover allowance against stopping time."}

Alongside these visual notes, unnumbered **marginal navigation pointers** trace architectural connections across chapters. Three symbols distinguish whether a pointer looks back to a foundation, ahead to a downstream consumer, or across to a contrasting design:

- **`↩` Backward pointer:** Directs the reader back to the earlier chapter where a physical bound, hardware contract, or clock cadence was established.
- **`↪` Forward pointer:** Directs the reader ahead to the later chapter, or to an appendix, where the idea is developed, measured, or enforced.
- **`⇄` Contrast:** Marks a place where two chapters or machine classes treat the same problem differently.

A pointer only orients. When an argument depends on another chapter, the reference stays in the text.

## What This Book Is Not {#sec-about-not}

This is not a ROS 2 or middleware manual. Middleware and messaging frameworks change, whereas the physical requirements they must satisfy (bounded latency, deterministic serialization, and fault isolation) do not. The book therefore introduces real-time protocols and message queues only as mechanisms to meet stated physical deadlines. Nor is it a mechanical CAD manual or a motor design treatise, because it characterizes actuators, transmissions, and thermal limits through the software budgets they impose rather than through their mechanical fabrication. For the same reason, simulation appears here not as a benchmark leaderboard, where open-loop scores stand in for deployment, but as a tool for generating hypotheses and training data. Its claims must still be verified on the physical machine. Software agents that act solely behind digital APIs without physical actuators remain outside our scope.

## A Note on Durability {#sec-about-durability}

Robot form factors, neural network architectures, and motor drive silicon will evolve, some before this book reaches print. The text therefore emphasizes the principles that survive those transitions: the causal boundary as the unit of engineering, the four governing laws, the separation between learned proposers and deterministic permission paths, and the discipline of grounding operational authority in empirical evidence. Current platforms and models appear throughout to make the concepts concrete, but the principles stand independently of any specific vendor, model, or hardware platform. Where a question is actively unsettled in the field, such as how best to verify generalist policies against rare corner cases, the book presents the problem as an open engineering challenge rather than settled doctrine.

## Prerequisites {#sec-about-prerequisites}

The worked examples and derivations draw on five foundational areas. Readers should be comfortable with:

- programming in Python and working with numeric arrays;
- core machine learning concepts, including supervised training, loss functions, and inference;
- introductory Newtonian mechanics (position, velocity, acceleration, force, torque, inertia);
- linear algebra (vectors, matrices, coordinate transformations); and
- undergraduate probability and basic statistics.

Deeper background in classical control theory, real-time operating systems, or robotics kinematics is beneficial but not required; the book develops the necessary control, estimation, and real-time concepts where they are first needed. Every specialized tool is introduced from first principles at the point where a concrete systems decision depends on it.
